title: Act IV, Scene VII

teacherSummary.text: Claudius explains to Laertes why he did not punish Hamlet publicly. News arrives that Hamlet has returned. They plot a fencing match with an unbated, poisoned sword and a poisoned cup. Gertrude reports Ophelia drowned.

vocabulary.context:
The queen his mother
Lives almost by his looks; and for myself—
My virtue or my plague, be it either which—
She’s so conjunctive to my life and soul,
That, as the star moves not but in his sphere,
I could not but by her.

I read “I will do’t: / And, for that purpose, I’ll anoint my sword” slowly and put it in my own words: Laertes agrees to Claudius's plan and adds that he will poison his sword. Next, craft. I notice he goes beyond Claudius's plan, adding his own treachery. The strongest word is “anoint”: it is a holy word for applying oil, here used for poison. Then, effect. What does Laertes agree to do? My answer: Laertes agrees to kill Hamlet in a fencing match with an unblunted, poisoned sword; his grief turns him into a schemer, and the plot sets up the deaths of Hamlet, Laertes, Gertrude and Claudius.
